newsitem.title: BOSNIA: NATO troops try to disperse voters angry at delay.
newsitem.headline: NATO troops try to disperse voters angry at delay.

text.p: NATO troops were sent to disperse a crowd of some 2,000 people outside polling stations in Sarajevo on Saturday after voters angry with delays kicked in doors and smashed windows, an alliance spokesman said.
Major Brett Boudreau told a news briefing the disturbances occurred when long queues developed outside polling stations in the densely populated high-rise Novi Grad district.

"There's been some damage done to eight polling stations. Some windows were broken and doors kicked in. Problems in all these locations appeared to be generated by the amount of time it takes for people to go through the voting process."

He said a French unit of the NATO-led peace Implementation Force (IFOR) as well as U.N. police monitors were dispatched to the district at the request of the election supervisors, the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe.
"OSCE requested IFOR assistance to help disperse the crowd. OSCE is also looking into establishing additional polling stations in the area," Boudreau said.
Jeff Fischer, the OSCE's elections' director, said all eight polling stations were closed temporarily shortly before midday to sort out unspecified organisational problems.
He said they would reopen and operate beyond the official 7 p.m. (1700 GMT) close of polling, possibly as late as 10 p.m. (2000 GMT), to make up for the lost time.

Some delays in polling on Bosnia's first post-war election day may have been caused by strict anti-fraud measures in which voters were being scanned with infra-red devices and their hands sprayed with invisible ink.
Some voters have also needed time for explanations of the secret-ballot procedure and a plethora of choices on separate ballot forms corresponding to four tiers of government.
Fischer said the OSCE would decide at 5 p.m. (1500 GMT) whether to keep polling stations open across Bosnia beyond the official 7 p.m. closing time.
OSCE officials have called the elections the most complex in history.
